_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 12 Secret Codes. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order: why ciphers, the 1 = a code, writing in code, reading code, plain text and ciphertext, and why a simple cipher can be broken. EVERY NUMBER ON SCREEN COMES FROM THE LESSON'S OWN RULE - the pictures call ART.code and ART.decode (computing.js codeWord/decodeCode), never a table typed into the film - and every word enciphered here is one the lesson itself enciphers: cat 3 1 20, bee 2 5 5, hat 8 1 20, hi 8 9, secret 19 5 3 18 5 20, code 3 15 4 5, hello 8 5 12 12 15. The cipher wheel is a closure in the kit and cannot be lifted, so the code strip is drawn here in the engine's idiom and filled from the rule.
title: Secret Codes
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Know that ciphers are a way of making sure that information stays secret.
Know how to write and decode messages using very simple code, including converting letters to numbers (1 = a, 2 = b, etc.).

beats.say: Send a message across a network, and many computers see it on the way.
A cipher turns cat into 3 1 20. Only the key turns it back into words.
A message on a network passes through many computers on its way.
Every one of them can see it. Without a cipher, they can read it too.
A cipher changes the message by a rule. Now it looks like nonsense.
Only the person with the rule can read it. That rule is the key.
A cipher does not hide your message. They can see it but not read it.
Passwords, bank details and private messages all travel this way.
The alphabet, a to z, is twenty-six letters long.
Give every letter its number. a is 1, b is 2, c is 3.
Keep counting all the way to z, which is 26.
Careful: j is 10, not 9. Count along the strip and you will not slip.
That rule, 1 is a and 2 is b, is the key to this cipher.
To write a word in code, take one letter at a time.

at.write: To write a word in code

beats.say: cat starts with c. Find c on the strip: c is 3.
Then a is 1, and t is 20. So cat in code is 3, 1, 20.
The same letter is always the same number.
So bee is 2, 5, 5. The e is 5 both times.
Decoding goes the other way. You start with the numbers.
To decode 8 9, find the eighth letter. It is h.
The ninth letter is i. So 8 9 says hi.
A longer one now: 19 5 3 18 5 20 says secret.
Without the key, 8 9 is just two numbers.
A message has two forms, and each one has its own name.
Before you do anything to it, the message is plain text.
Now apply the rule. What comes out is called ciphertext.
hat is the plain text. 8 1 20 is the same message as ciphertext.
Apply the rule the other way, and you get the plain text back.

scenes.heading: Why this cipher can be broken

beats.say: The same letter is always the same number. That makes it easy to use.
It is also its weakness. Count the numbers in a long coded message.
The one that turns up most is probably e. In English, e is the commonest letter.
Somebody can start there and work out the rest. They never needed the key.
A cipher changes a message by a rule. That rule is the key.
Encode cat and you get 3 1 20. Decode 8 9 and you get hi.
Plain text goes in, ciphertext comes out, and without the key it is nonsense.
